pr_body:
Implement directives `NoExecPaths=` and `ExecPaths=` to control `MS_NOEXEC`
mount flag for the file system tree. This can be used to implement file system
W^X policies, and for example with allow-listing mode (`NoExecPaths=/`) a
compromised service would not be able to execute a shell, if that was not
explicitly allowed.

Example:
[Service]
NoExecPaths=/
ExecPaths=/usr/bin/daemon /usr/lib64 /usr/lib

Fixes #17942
pr_comments:
I've applied in my system a generic policy below as a drop-in to all services (except for interactive user programs, `user@.service`, `user-runtime-directory@.service`):
```
[Service]
NoExecPaths=/
ExecPaths=-/usr/bin -/usr/lib -/usr/lib64 -/usr/libexec -/usr/sbin
RootImageOptions=root:nodev,noexec,nosuid
```

For user programs to work, this additional drop-in seems to be enough:
```
[Service]
ExecPaths=-/dev/shm -/home -/run/user -/setuid -/usr/games
```

Package installer wants to run scripts in /etc and /var/lib/dpkg.

hmm, the code doesn't know how to handle if I list the same dir in both NoExecPaths= and ReadOnlyPaths=, no? i.e. this smells like needing some bigger updates namespace.c so that in that case entries are merged with both flags.

(And given that the nosymlinks flag has recently been added this will be more than just two-dimensional sooner or later)

> hmm, the code doesn't know how to handle if I list the same dir in both NoExecPaths= and ReadOnlyPaths=, no? i.e. this smells like needing some bigger updates namespace.c so that in that case entries are merged with both flags.

Right, there seems to be some interference.

> (And given that the nosymlinks flag has recently been added this will be more than just two-dimensional sooner or later)

What's that, can you elaborate a bit?

> > (And given that the nosymlinks flag has recently been added this will be more than just two-dimensional sooner or later)
> 
> What's that, can you elaborate a bit?

MS_NOSYMFOLLOW is a new flag that turns off symlink following on a mount point.
commit message misses a `#` in the fixes line

The kernel commit for MS_NOSYMFOLLOW is [dab741e0e02bd3c4](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/torvalds/linux.git/commit/?id=dab741e0e02bd3c4). It could be enabled with something like `NoSymlinkFollowPaths=` for each path item for fine control, but perhaps it's enough to enable it for all mounts (`NoSymlinkFollow=yes` for the whole service). The theory would be that either the service can live without symlinks, or it doesn't. Though for example on Debian, I think files may change to symlinks if a new package enters the pool and "alternatives" system is enabled for the files. With "alternatives" it's possible to install for example several packages providing "vi", like "vim", "nvi" etc. and the administrator can choose which of them is started when "vi" is invoked. This could be broken with the fine-grained approach too.

I settled for user services with this drop-in:
```
[Service]
ExecPaths=-/dev/shm -/etc -/home -/run/user -/setuid -/usr
```
It's not so tight policy as I'd like (executable content seems to be everywhere), but seems to work. It still turns on noexec for /dev (except /dev/shm), /boot, /proc, /run (except /run/user), /sys, /tmp and /var.

We need to be careful with the nosymlink flag, as if it's not supported at runtime the kernel will just silently discard it and carry on mounting without it. Which is really not great for a security flag...

issue_context.title: Feature: noexec (or mount flag) controls
issue_context.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
With #17940 the default mount flags for `/dev` would change to allow executable files. To allow hardening the system with strict W^X file system policies for services, it should be possible to change the default on a case by case basis. Today, typically services don't need exec access to `/dev` at all, but this may change if Intel SGX gains acceptance.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
The mount flags for a path should be changeable for individual services with new directives like:
- `NoExecPaths=/dev` (matches `ReadOnlyPaths=`, `InaccessiblePaths=`)
- `MountOptions=/dev:rw,noexec,dev,nosuid` (generic mount option directive)
- `ProtectDev=yes` (higher level control but specific to `/dev`, could include other features in the future)
- `RestrictSGX=yes` (very specific to SGX)
- `RestrictEnclaves=yes` (less specific to SGX)
comments:
One more idea:
- `FileSystemDenyWriteExecute=yes` (like `MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes`)

The idea would be that for W&X paths, either write access or execute access would be removed, according to heuristics. It's not so clear what those could be though.

With `NoExecPaths=` and the reverse directive `ExecPaths=`, allow-listing of all executable content could be implemented:
```
[Service]
NoExecPaths=/
ExecPaths=/usr/sbin/daemon /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 /usr/lib 
```
This would not be possible with `MountOptions=` without considering the possible mount options for each file system.

@poettering @keszybz any preference? Most of the possible options are not mutually exclusive, so more than one could be implemented.

Every new option we add comes at a price: the burden to maintain it. In particular stuff that is opt-in comes at a very high price. 

I am not sure MS_NOEXEC on /dev/ is really worth the effort and burden. I mean, I am all for locking things down, if we can do it without compromising too hard. But I am not sure that it's really worth locking this down, it doesn't really substantially reduce attack surface afaics, but it's very nichey.

I agree that only MS_NOEXEC for only `/dev` would indeed be too nichey (something like `NoExecDev=yes`) and that's why I'm proposing more generic or higher level controls.

I think `NoExecPaths=` (complemented with `ExecPaths=`) would be the most generally useful of the list of ideas above. Controlling execute permissions across all file systems with allow-listing would be very powerful. For example, it could mean that a compromised service would not be able to execute a shell, if that was not explicitly allowed. The execute permissions for writable locations may also be easily controlled with allow-listing mode.

We've also discussed about something like `MountOptions=` before, but I think for this case it would not be the best tool.
